teaser: Map every layer from the hardware to the business contract by who signs it; the lines nobody signs are the blind spots worth paying to see.
core_idea: A maintainer's signature names who stands behind a version, not what is running; extending Andrey Lazarev's split between measured and declared context, every layer from hardware to business contract should end in an accountable signer, forming a fractal graph of signed certificates in which unsigned lines are visible blind spots for businesses and insurers to accept or close, with experts paid to sign and departures exposed.

figures.caption: Who signs for each layer: an accountability map from the business to the hardware. Each line says what is claimed, whether it is measured or declared, and who signs it: the business owner for the contract, the product owner for what was delivered, a maintainer for the code that goes live and the release, the platform team for the process, the cloud provider for the platform, a hardware root and a verifier for the device. The building, who can reach it and what is plugged in, is signed by nobody: a blind spot. An illustration of the argument, not an audit of any system.

The LinkedIn thread under my post sharing "Who maintains the PHP you run?", 24 October 2026: Andrey Lazarev on what a maintainer's signature does and does not prove, my replies, and his split between what a device can measure and what an operator or auditor has to declare.

Every signed line is a graph of its own: the line "the device: this is what actually booted", signed by a verifier, opens into the measurement, the reference it should match, the verifier who checked one against the other, and the endorsement of the hardware root. The same holds in every domain: the business, the product, the code, the release, the platform, the device. Each opening ends in somebody who signed, or in a blind spot.
